questions.question: Why do 1 molal glucose and 1 molal urea solutions show nearly the same boiling-point elevation, while 1 molal NaCl shows nearly double?
questions.solution: Colligative properties count PARTICLES, not identities. Glucose and urea are non-electrolytes: 1 mol gives 1 mol of particles. NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ + Cl⁻, so i ≈ 2 — twice the particles, twice the ΔTb. The van't Hoff factor i is the multiplier; dissociation, not the solute's identity, drives the difference.

questions.question: Why do the colligative-property formulas use molality instead of molarity?
questions.solution: Molality = mol solute per kg SOLVENT — both masses are temperature-independent. Molarity divides by solution VOLUME, which expands on heating, so a molarity-based ΔTb would itself drift with temperature and make the 'constant' Kb ill-defined. Temperature-independent ratios are the requirement.

questions.question: A solution of A and B shows a vapour pressure LOWER than Raoult's law predicts. What interaction does this signal, and what happens to the mixing enthalpy and volume?
questions.solution: Negative deviation: A–B attractions are STRONGER than the average of A–A and B–B, so molecules escape less easily — P < P_Raoult. Stronger attraction means mixing releases energy (ΔH_mix < 0) and the molecules pull together (ΔV_mix < 0). Chloroform + acetone is the standard example (hydrogen bonding). Positive deviation is the mirror image.

questions.question: Why does a raisin swell in fresh water but a raisin in saturated sugar solution shrinks? Name the driving quantity.
questions.solution: Water moves through the semipermeable membrane from LOWER to HIGHER solute concentration (lower to higher osmotic pressure region). Fresh water outside: water flows in — swelling. Saturated sugar outside: water flows out — shrinking. The driving quantity is the osmotic-pressure DIFFERENCE (π = iCRT) across the membrane.

questions.question: A soda bottle fizzes violently when opened but only slowly when left uncapped. Explain with Henry's law, including the temperature factor.
questions.solution: Henry's law: p = K_H·x — gas solubility is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid. Bottled: high CO₂ pressure keeps large x. Opened: p drops to 0.0004 atm, solubility collapses, CO₂ escapes. Warming the drink raises K_H (solubility falls), so warm soda goes flat faster — the K_H temperature trend is the extra mark.

questions.question: Why can fractional distillation never purify 95% ethanol beyond its azeotrope, no matter how many plates?
questions.solution: An azeotrope is a composition where the liquid and vapour have the SAME composition — the mixture boils and condenses as one substance. At that point relative volatility is exactly 1: each vaporisation-condensation cycle changes nothing, so more plates cannot shift the composition. Breaking it needs a third component (entrainer) or a different separation principle.

questions.concept: Depression of freezing point — the mechanism
questions.question: Explain why adding salt to ice lowers the freezing point, in terms of vapour pressure — not just 'salt melts ice'.
questions.solution: At 0 °C ice and pure water have equal vapour pressure (equilibrium). Dissolved salt lowers the LIQUID's vapour pressure (Raoult), so ice now has the higher vapour pressure and melts to restore equilibrium — melting absorbs heat and the mixture cools. The equilibrium-shift framing, not 'salt is warm', is the correct mechanism.

questions.question: Benzoic acid in benzene shows a molar mass nearly DOUBLE its formula mass. What is happening, and how does the van't Hoff factor capture it?
questions.solution: Benzoic acid dimerises in benzene via hydrogen bonding: 2 molecules act as one particle, so the particle count halves and the measured (colligative) molar mass doubles. i = actual particles/formula units = 0.5 here. Association (i < 1) raises apparent molar mass; dissociation (i > 1) lowers it — the two cases the examiner pairs.
